profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-affiliated medical center in Taipei is preparing a policy-oriented grant concept and conference symposium proposal based on an 8-year analysis of NHIA reimbursement decisions for innovative medical devices in Taiwan. The brainstorming meeting is between the health economics lead and a senior clinician who sits on the hospital's new technology committee. Their agenda is to generate possible follow-up analyses and policy recommendations that could make the prior findings more actionable for regulators and hospitals, especially around delayed reimbursement decisions, use of local real-world data, and the handling of special medical devices. The expected outcome is a short list of 3-4 promising study angles and policy ideas to develop into a grant concept note and presentation abstract.

members.name: Dr. Mei-Ling Lin
members.role: Associate Professor of Health Economics and HTA Research Lead
members.expertise: Reimbursement policy analysis, claims-based outcomes research, PBRS/NHIA process mapping
members.background: Trained in pharmacy and health policy, Dr. Lin has led several academic studies using NHIA public lists, reimbursement files, and meeting minutes to examine adoption timelines for new technologies.
members.private_state: She wants the follow-up project to produce a regulator-facing framework that is methodologically publishable and feasible with secondary data plus a small qualitative component, while avoiding a design that depends on hard-to-access hospital operational data.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing 'patient access,' the most policy-relevant and measurable access point is the NHIA reimbursement decision date, because that is when broad insured uptake becomes possible.

References to 'the 2013 regulation' reasonably bundle the formal regulation and the associated review architecture introduced around that time into one policy period starting with applications filed after late 2012.

If the team proposes using 'local real-world data,' the realistic meaning is Taiwan-generated evidence that can be assembled before or during reimbursement review from claims, registries, or chart abstraction on comparable use patterns.
A practical recommendation to 'speed up the review' should be evaluated against administrative timeline measures such as application-to-decision days rather than hospital-level procurement timing.

members.name: Dr. Yu-Han Chen
members.role: Senior Interventional Cardiologist and Hospital New Technology Committee Liaison
members.expertise: Introduction of implantable cardiovascular devices, hospital technology adoption, clinician-industry-regulator interface
members.background: Dr. Chen leads structural heart and complex coronary programs at a tertiary medical center and regularly works with hospital procurement and device companies on bringing in new devices before or during reimbursement review.
members.private_state: He wants the project to highlight the real clinical bottlenecks he experiences—especially delayed routine availability after hospitals already know a device works—and to produce recommendations that could justify earlier conditional use for high-need patients.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing 'patient access,' the meaningful access point is when a patient at a major center can actually receive the device through self-pay, compassionate use, trial channels, or special hospital arrangements, not only when national reimbursement is granted.

When people mention 'the 2013 regulation,' they usually mean the stricter practical review environment that clinicians felt after later operational changes and tougher committee expectations, not merely the text of the original rule.

Using 'local real-world data' naturally implies evidence collected after limited clinical introduction in Taiwan under a provisional or conditional arrangement, because that is the only convincing local evidence for truly novel devices.

If the group says the process should be 'faster,' the important test is whether a device can enter real clinical use within the same budget cycle at tertiary centers, even if formal NHIA timestamps do not change much.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the regulation delayed 'patient access' to innovative devices.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means access begins when NHIA reimbursement approval is issued, since that enables scalable insured availability and can be observed consistently in reimbursement records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means access begins when patients at advanced hospitals can actually receive the device through self-pay, trial, compassionate, or ad hoc hospital pathways, even before reimbursement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In policy and clinical conversations alike, 'access' sounds shared and value-laden, so both can endorse improving it without noticing they anchor the term to different operational starting points.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the 2013 regulation' as the policy change whose impact they want to unpack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the formal reimbursement regulation introduced around late 2012/2013 and treats all subsequent cases as part of the same post-regulation regime.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally referring to the later, stricter review climate that emerged after subsequent PBRS/NHIA operational tightening, which he experienced as the real turning point.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are pointing to the same broad reform era and neither is likely to stop a brainstorming flow to specify exact circulars, implementation dates, or committee workflow revisions.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'local real-world data' would be used for
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both propose bringing in 'local real-world data' to support reimbursement decisions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means pre-decision evidence packages built from Taiwan claims, disease registries, or retrospective chart review that can inform the reimbursement review itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means collecting outcome data after provisional entry or limited early use in Taiwan, then using those local results to justify broader reimbursement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds highly aligned and technically sophisticated, and in brainstorming people often endorse it without separating whether the evidence is meant to precede, accompany, or follow initial access.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'faster review process' should accomplish
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the review process should be made 'faster' or 'simplified.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 would count success as shortening measurable application-to-NHIA-decision time or reducing administrative steps in the documented review sequence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 would count success as letting hospitals begin routine use within one budgeting cycle, even if the official decision clock is partly unchanged because practical entry barriers are reduced.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'faster' appears self-explanatory, and each person's criterion feels like the obvious real-world meaning from their role, so neither sees a need to unpack how speed would actually be assessed.

turns.inner_thought: Our 8-year dataset is strongest on formal reimbursement milestones, committee sequence, and decision timing. If we position the follow-up around how the 2013 regulation changed patient access, I mean access from reimbursement approval onward, because that is observable and policy-relevant at scale. I also want to keep the design feasible with secondary data and maybe a few interviews, not drift into hospital operational records we cannot systematically obtain. And when we talk about simplifying the review path, I want that anchored to documented administrative steps and measurable application-to-decision days.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From the 8-year analysis, the broad picture is clear: innovative devices moved through a longer and more layered reimbursement pathway over time, and the next step is to explain more concretely how the 2013 regulation affected patient access and what kinds of changes might simplify the review path. Ideally, we come out of today with three or four angles that can work for both a grant concept and the symposium abstract.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that framing works. From my side, what matters is when patients can actually get the device in a major center, not when the paperwork reaches a national endpoint. And when she says the 2013 regulation, I naturally think of the more conservative review environment that clinicians really started feeling later, not just the original rule text. I should keep it practical and emphasize availability in real clinical settings.
turns.utterance: I agree. From the clinical side, the most compelling story is the waiting time before these devices were actually available in practice after the 2013 regulation tightened. That is where the patient impact is most tangible, and I think people at the conference will immediately understand why it matters.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's aligned on access delays. I can turn that into a sequence analysis using the reimbursement files and committee documents. If we stratify by nonreimbursement code category and review path after the post-2012/2013 policy shift, we can estimate which formal steps are contributing the most time before reimbursement. That gives us something regulators can act on.
turns.utterance: One idea would be to stratify the cases by nonreimbursement code category and then map the post-2013 review sequence in more detail. We might be able to identify which parts of that sequence added the most delay to access, rather than treating the process as one single block.

turns.inner_thought: Special devices are exactly where the real bottleneck is. Clinically, many of these were ready to use long before hospitals could make them part of routine care. If this project is going to be useful, it should speak to the gap between readiness and real-world availability, especially within hospital budgeting realities. I won't over-specify that; 'access problems' will be enough.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I would put special medical devices near the center of the proposal. Those are often the cases where the technology is clinically ready well before hospitals can use it routinely, so if we want to show where the access problem is most serious, that seems like the right place to focus.

turns.inner_thought: A second package on local real-world data could be very publishable if we define feasible sources: Taiwan claims, registries, maybe retrospective chart review. My assumption is pre-decision or during-review evidence that reduces uncertainty in committee deliberation. And if we say faster review, I mean fewer days in the formal review clock. This stays within reachable data and regulator-facing recommendations.
turns.utterance: A second work package could look at whether bringing in local real-world data might make the reimbursement review faster, perhaps by reducing uncertainty in the committee process. That could give us a concrete policy recommendation rather than only describing delay.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. The persuasive local evidence is what comes after limited early use in Taiwan—once a few centers start using the device, we can show actual outcomes and then strengthen the reimbursement case. That's the bridge I care about. I assume she means the same by local real-world data, so I'll reinforce the idea without spelling out all the provisional-entry mechanics.
turns.utterance: I think that would be very persuasive. Local real-world data carries weight, especially if centers can begin with limited use and then feed Taiwan outcomes back into the reimbursement discussion. That makes the whole conversation much more grounded.

turns.inner_thought: Limited use aside, for the study design I need feasible data assembly methods that do not depend on opening hospital introduction pathways. I can broaden his point into practical sources we could actually propose: claims linkage, chart review, registries. If we frame it carefully, it still sounds fully aligned with his suggestion while keeping the evidence package squarely within accessible datasets.
turns.utterance: Right, and from a methods standpoint we could make that fairly concrete. We might discuss claims linkage, retrospective chart review, and existing registries as feasible ways to assemble local evidence, then translate that into a recommendation for how the review could use it more systematically.

turns.inner_thought: Good. But the proposal also has to say something hospitals care about. If the pathway is not faster in practice, we still lose a year because budgeting windows close and the device never becomes routine. For me the test is whether a center can bring it into use within the same cycle, not whether some official interval is modestly shorter. I'll keep it at the level of a faster pathway so she hears it as shared.
turns.utterance: I also think the practical side should be very visible in the proposal. We should recommend a faster pathway so hospitals do not miss an entire annual budgeting cycle before innovative devices reach patients. That point will resonate strongly with both clinicians and administrators.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I can operationalize that as shorter application-to-decision time, maybe even quantify how many days could be saved by removing or consolidating certain formal steps. That gives us a hard endpoint and lets us frame improved patient access under the regulation in a way regulators will accept. I should present it as complementing his point.
turns.utterance: Agreed. On the analytic side, we could measure whether a faster pathway might shave several hundred days off application-to-decision time and frame that as improved patient access under the regulation. If we can show where those days accumulate, the recommendations become much more actionable.

turns.inner_thought: I still want to distinguish the earlier years from the later, tougher climate that we all felt in submissions. That's what I think of when people mention the 2013 regulation in practice. If we compare those phases, it may validate clinicians' experience without forcing me to litigate exact policy documents right now.
turns.utterance: It may also help to contrast the early post-2013 years with the later period when the review atmosphere became noticeably more conservative for new device submissions. Clinically, that shift felt quite real, and I suspect it is part of the story.

turns.inner_thought: That makes sense as a within-era split. I can keep the whole post-late-2012/2013 architecture as one regulatory regime, then divide it into earlier and later cohorts using NHIA and PBRS records. No need to disentangle multiple policy events unless the data force it. This is still tractable and publishable.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can treat that as a split within the same overall post-regulation period and compare earlier versus later cohorts using NHIA and PBRS records. That would let us test whether the pattern changed over time without losing the main policy narrative.

turns.inner_thought: This is coming together. For the concept note, I want the emphasis to stay on patient access in real clinical settings, local real-world data that supports broader uptake after initial use, and a faster review model that actually works for special devices in major centers. She seems on the same page, so we can leave the details for later drafting.
turns.utterance: That sounds good to me. For the final concept note, I would emphasize patient access, local real-world data, and a faster review model that is realistic for special device introduction in major centers. If we structure it that way, I think it will speak to regulators, hospitals, and clinicians at the same time.
